title: Origami as a Spatial and Geometric Reasoning Benchmark
abstract: Multimodal language models perform well on visual recognition and on tool use, but these abilities do not transfer directly to spatial and geometric reasoning. Geometric structure does not reduce to text or to a single image: exact angles and incidences, which surface lies in front of which, and the order in which operations were applied are not recoverable from a semantic description of a scene. We introduce CP2Seq, a benchmark for evaluating geometric reasoning and sequential planning in multimodal language models through origami. The benchmark contains 600 procedurally generated samples, each requiring a model to produce a valid sequence of folds from a crease pattern and a target folded state. Samples are produced by a deterministic folding engine. Ground truth is recorded during generation. We release the generation and evaluation framework to support additional samples and experiments across reference depths and action models. During evaluation, the engine executes proposed folds or rejects invalid actions with explicit feedback, while the model remains responsible for selecting actions and searching for a solution. We evaluate multimodal language models under progressively greater tool assistance, and against a deterministic breadth-first search over the same action set. Candidate sequences are assessed by executing them and comparing the resulting folded state with the target, allowing for planar translations, rotations, and reflections. Performance falls off sharply with sequence depth: in the Luna ablations no configuration solves a medium or hard sample (11 or more folds), while some-layers solves rise from 6/30 to 18/30 with higher reasoning effort. Failures are dominated by search rather than by illegal moves: in the broader evaluation, 48% of episodes end by revisiting earlier states. A breadth-first search over the same actions, under its own time budget, solves 54.7% of easy-group attempts, so short sequences are within reach of systematic search.

title: Beyond Benchmark Accuracy: A Hybrid Framework for Phishing URL and Email Detection
abstract: Phishing detectors can achieve almost perfect accuracy on benchmark datasets and still struggle with the links people encounter in practice. This paper investigates that gap and describes a hybrid framework for assessing URLs and emails through machine learning, language analysis, header inspection, and transparent rules. Our URL model combines character-level TF-IDF with 17 lexical features in a logistic regression classifier. Analysis of the 235,795 URLs in PhiUSIIL revealed pronounced differences in how the two classes were represented: every legitimate example used a simple HTTPS domain format, while 59.9% of phishing URLs included a path and 51.3% used HTTP. A classifier trained on raw URLs achieved 99.71% test accuracy, yet incorrectly marked 26 of 30 ordinary legitimate links as phishing. To limit reliance on these patterns, we trained a second classifier on 197,591 unique registered domains. On held-out domains, it achieved 86.02% accuracy, a ROC-AUC of 0.892, and 89.02% phishing precision. We then combined its predictions with URL-pattern checks, NLTK-based email cues, and SPF, DKIM, and DMARC evidence in a Flask prototype that reports a risk score and supporting reasons. The results show why dataset composition and realistic tests matter as much as headline accuracy when evaluating phishing detection.

title: Spacetime: A Library for Cleaning and Combining Disparate Spatiotemporal Datasets in Python
abstract: As climate change accelerates, spatiotemporal climate and weather data rasters are increasingly used in academic research, agriculture, infrastructure, and other disci-plines across public and private domains. Unfortunately, these raster data are often stored under numerous file types with different spatial and temporal boundaries, spa-tial reference systems, and spatial and temporal resolutions. The tools and workflows that we have are often hindered by coordinate reference system mismatches, data type mismatches, data aggregation mismatches, and other fundamental challenges. To fully harness the impacts of these data, software tools are needed that can be leveraged effi-ciently and intuitively and without a steep learning curve for the new user. In this pa-per, we introduce Spacetime, a novel programming library in Python that enables effi-cient spatiotemporal data processing, management, alignment, and analysis. Spacetime is an open-source project written in Python that provides a set of powerful functions to manipulate spatiotemporal data in a single, unified library. Spacetime’s overarching themes are simplicity and usability. However, the library does not com-promise processing speed. In our comparison, it was as fast or faster than other popu-lar Python libraries, while requiring many fewer lines of code and no external loops or control functions. We hope this library will lower the barrier of entry to scientists in fields that have not traditionally used spatiotemporal raster data but are doing so in-creasingly frequently in the current climate.
